playbook:
# Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an unowned property, I assess whether to buy based on:
- Can I afford it without depleting my cash reserves below 50?
- Is it early enough in the game (lap 1-3) that the property will generate rent across multiple remaining laps?
- If both conditions are met, buy. If either fails, pass.

Early acquisition of low-to-mid price properties (50-80 range) is preferable to high-price properties (100+) because early properties will generate multiple rounds of incoming rent before the game ends. On lap 1-2, I should buy solid mid-tier properties like Wharf (price 80, rent 18) to establish an income stream.

Properties that cost exactly my remaining cash (120 on lap 2 when holding 120) should be declined even if the math looks neutral—zero reserves create unnecessary debt risk and eliminate my ability to respond to future unexpected costs.

When I land on an opponent's property and owe rent, I pay immediately without negotiation or deferral. I note the expense and adjust my balance accordingly.

When I pass START, I collect my salary and add it to my declared balance without fail.

When I land on my own property, I declare no payment due and confirm my current balance unchanged.

On the final lap (lap 6 of 6), do not buy unowned properties. Properties purchased on the final lap generate zero incoming rent, making any purchase cost a pure loss. Cash on hand at game end is worth more than unowned deeds.

From lap 4 onward, become increasingly selective about property acquisition. The remaining number of laps must justify the upfront cost through expected rent collection. A property costing 70 on lap 5 or 6 is not worth buying.

Track all transactions with precision. Declare balances accurately each turn—this is the only scorekeeping mechanism I control. Include the salary received when passing START in my balance calculation.

The winning metric is highest declared cash plus purchase price of owned deeds. Owning multiple properties with low cash on hand is not necessarily better than owning one property with high cash reserves. Balance portfolio value against liquid reserves.

# Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an owned property, I pay the rent without hesitation if I have the cash. Rent payments are mandatory and I should never try to avoid them.

When I land on an unowned property, I evaluate whether to buy based on my current cash position and the remaining laps. I should buy properties strategically in the early laps when I have capital available.

When I have enough cash to buy an unowned property and multiple laps remain (at least 3), I should buy it. Properties generate steady rent income and my final score includes both cash and deed values.

When I lack sufficient cash to buy an unowned property, I pass without agonizing over it. This is straightforward.

When I pass START, I always collect my salary. This is free money.

When it's the final lap or final two laps (lap 5-6/6), I do not buy properties since there is no time to recoup the investment or collect meaningful rent from other players.

I track my cash balance carefully and declare it accurately each turn. My final score is the sum of declared cash plus the purchase price of deeds I hold.

I recognize that buying two properties early (Foundry and Exchange for 220 total) and collecting consistent rent from opponents was effective. The rent income (24 from investor 2 on Foundry, 30 from investor 2 on Exchange) compounded my advantage. My final score of 339 reflects both my deed holdings and cash position.

Next time, I should continue this pattern: acquire 2-3 mid-to-high-value properties in laps 1-3 while I have capital, then rely on rent income to sustain or grow my cash in later laps. This strategy balances liquidity with deed value maximization.

I should avoid the temptation to hold cash passively. If I have funds available in the early laps and a property is reasonably priced (under 120), I should buy it to start collecting rent sooner.

2.text:
# PLAYBOOK FOR REF_ESTATE__SHIPPED

When I land on an unowned property early in the game (laps 1-3), I buy it if I have the cash available. Properties generate steady income across multiple laps, and early acquisition compounds my advantage.

When I land on an unowned property in the middle game (laps 3-4) and I lack sufficient cash, I decline the purchase rather than overextend myself. A cash cushion prevents me from being unable to pay rent later.

When I land on an unowned property in the late game (lap 5+), I evaluate whether the purchase price leaves me with enough liquidity to handle rent obligations in the final lap. On lap 5 specifically, I buy if I can afford it and still have a reasonable cushion—I need cash for rent on the final lap, not just enough to barely buy.

When I pass START, I always collect my salary—this is automatic income that improves my final score.

When I owe rent, I pay it immediately and accurately, calculating my new balance including all recent income received.

When calculating my balance, I account for: last declared balance + any rent I received + any salary collected - any rent owed - any purchase made. I verify this math before declaring.

My final score is determined by my declared cash balance plus the purchase prices of the deeds I hold, so I track both components. Do not let low cash alone discourage me—properties I own have value in the score calculation.

I do not buy property on the final lap since there is no opportunity to collect rent from it before scoring.

I should be more aggressive about acquiring properties early. In lap 3, I had 146 in cash and bought the Mill for 90—this was a good decision. I should continue this strategy in future games, as properties provide both insurance against bankruptcy and value at final scoring.

Investor 1 dominated this game by acquiring three high-value properties (Foundry, Exchange, and Wharf) in the first two laps. I should recognize when one investor is accumulating properties and prioritize acquiring the remaining unowned properties before they do.
